STRONGLY WOKE

The Boys

✅ NOT A WOKE TRAP

The Boys does not qualify as a woke trap under VVWS v1.1. A woke trap requires ideological content that remains hidden past 50 percent of the runtime, using a traditional-seeming or apolitical exterior to lure in audiences before revealing a progressive agenda. The Boys is openly, aggressively political from the first episode. The name of the game is stated in the premiere title itself. Homelander wears an American flag as a cape while being a narcissistic murderer. Vought International is immediately established as a soulless corporation commodifying human beings. The Deep sexually assaults Starlight within the first hour. None of this is subtle. None of it is hidden. The show wears its politics on its blood-splattered sleeve and has never pretended otherwise. Audiences who arrived expecting traditional superhero fare had only themselves to blame for not reading the room.

Our Verdict on The Boys

The Boys is a show that knows exactly what it thinks of you, your values, your country, your favorite superheroes, and your media consumption habits. It does not like most of them. Season 1 is a brutally effective piece of entertainment that arrives at the peak of Marvel saturation with a simple proposition: what if superheroes were real, and being real meant they were awful?

Eric Kripke's adaptation of Garth Ennis's comic series takes place in a world where superpowered individuals, called 'supes,' are managed by Vought International, a pharmaceutical-cum-entertainment conglomerate that discovered, weaponized, and monetized the Compound V serum that creates them. The Seven are Vought's crown jewels, a Justice League analog whose public image is meticulously stage-managed while their private behavior ranges from negligent to monstrous. Homelander (Antony Starr) is the Superman figure, draped in the American flag, beloved by millions, and utterly hollow inside. His public smile has the warmth of a stock photo. In private, he murders people who inconvenience him and nurses a pathological need for maternal approval from his corporate handler, Madelyn Stillwell (Elisabeth Shue).

The show's dual-protagonist structure works beautifully. Hughie Campbell (Jack Quaid) is an electronics store clerk whose girlfriend Robin is liquefied by A-Train (Jessie T. Usher), a speedster who was literally running through her while high on his own brand of Compound V. Hughie's journey from shock to grief to recruitment by Billy Butcher (Karl Urban) is the show's emotional spine. Meanwhile, Annie January (Erin Moriarty), a genuine small-town hero who calls herself Starlight, achieves her lifelong dream of joining the Seven only to discover on her first day that the dream is a nightmare. The Deep (Chace Crawford) sexually assaults her in the second episode, and her subsequent arc through the season is about navigating a workplace where the predators are also her heroes.

Butcher is the show's most complicated figure. Karl Urban plays him as a shambling Cockney force of nature, equal parts charming and terrifying. He recruits Hughie not out of sympathy but because Hughie is useful. Butcher's vendetta against Homelander is personal in ways the season finale reveals with genuine shock. Urban makes Butcher compelling without making him likable, which is the right call. You should not like Billy Butcher. The show does not want you to like Billy Butcher. It wants you to recognize that fighting monsters requires becoming something monstrous, and to feel uncomfortable about that recognition.

Antony Starr's Homelander is the performance around which the entire show orbits. It is one of the great television villain performances of the streaming era. Starr plays Homelander as a man who has never faced a consequence in his life and has therefore never developed anything resembling a conscience. His neediness is more disturbing than his cruelty. He desperately wants to be loved while being incapable of love. The scenes where he hovers on the edge of violence, face twitching between personas, are genuinely tense in a way superhero media almost never achieves.

The show's production values belie its satirical intent. This looks like a real superhero show. The visual effects, locations, and cinematography invest fully in the world-building. The corporate sheen of Vought Tower, the grimy basements where the Boys plan their operations, the stadium rallies, the Christian festivals, the sex clubs: every environment is realized with conviction. You cannot effectively deconstruct a genre without demonstrating mastery of it, and The Boys demonstrates mastery.

Now, the ideological audit. The Boys is one of the most aggressively woke mainstream shows ever produced. This is not a criticism. It is a factual description that helps viewers decide whether the show is for them. The show's political commitments are not subtext. They are text. Vought International is the Military Industrial Media Complex collapsed into one building. Its products are superheroes. Its strategy is manufactured consent. Its internal culture is sexual predation. Its public relations strategy is performative patriotism. The show believes that corporations are evil, that celebrity culture is a control mechanism, that the American military is an instrument of corporate profit, that organized religion is a branding exercise for hypocrites, that masculinity as traditionally understood is toxic, and that the superhero genre itself is propaganda for a set of values the show rejects.

The Deep storyline in particular is a sustained critique of male sexual entitlement and workplace predation. The Christian superhero festival subplot with Ezekiel is a direct attack on religious hypocrisy. Homelander's flag cape is not an accident. Madelyn Stillwell's entire character is a study in corporate amorality dressed in power suits. The show's worldview is comprehensive and consistent.

What keeps The Boys from being purely a political lecture is craft. The writing is sharp. The performances are exceptional. The plotting is tightly structured across eight episodes. The show is genuinely funny in ways that do not depend on ideology. Frenchie (Tomer Capone) and Mother's Milk (Laz Alonso) provide texture and relief. Kimiko (Karen Fukuhara), introduced in episode 4 as a feral, superpowered young woman the Boys rescue, becomes the show's emotional sleeper weapon. Her wordless performance in episode 4 is devastating.

The traditional elements are present but outweighed. Hughie is motivated by love and grief. His father (Simon Pegg) is a genuinely sympathetic parent trying to protect his son. Starlight's moral integrity is presented as genuinely admirable, not naive. The Boys themselves, for all their moral compromises, are fighting to protect innocent people from unchecked power. These are traditional values. The show does not mock them. It just believes that the institutions that supposedly uphold those values are fraudulent.

For conservative viewers: you will be insulted by this show. It has nothing good to say about anything you hold dear. It believes patriotism is a marketing strategy, religion is hypocrisy, corporations are death machines, and traditional masculinity is a pathology. If you can watch a show that holds those beliefs because the writing, acting, and craft are exceptional, The Boys rewards the discomfort. If you cannot sit through eight hours of a show that thinks you are the problem, skip it.

The season finale, 'You Found Me,' upends everything. The reveal that Butcher's wife Becca is alive and has been kept secret by Vought for eight years, raising Homelander's son, recontextualizes Butcher's entire motivation. The revelation that Homelander created supervillains by dosing terrorists with Compound V to manufacture a threat only he could stop recontextualizes the show's entire political framework. It is a genuinely great season finale.

Season 1 of The Boys is peak prestige genre television made by people who despise what you love. It is well-made, well-acted, and ideologically cohesive propaganda. Whether you consider that a compliment or an indictment determines whether you should watch it.

Creative Team Deep Dive

Director: Eric Kripke (Showrunner/Creator)

LEFT. Kripke is openly progressive and has explicitly described The Boys as political satire. In interviews he has stated that if viewers cannot see that Homelander is the villain, they are watching the show wrong. He created Supernatural (2005-2020), a show that grew increasingly progressive over its 15-season run, moving from monster-of-the-week horror to explicit social commentary. Kripke has said in multiple interviews that The Boys is about the danger of celebrity worship, the corruption of unchecked corporate power, and the specific threat of performative patriotism masking authoritarian impulses. He is not hiding his politics. The show is exactly what he intended it to be.

Eric Kripke is an American television writer and producer born in 1974 in Toledo, Ohio. He created Supernatural for The WB/CW in 2005, serving as showrunner for its first five seasons and remaining an executive producer through its 15-season run. Supernatural began as a horror-fantasy series about two brothers hunting monsters and evolved into a sprawling franchise with a devoted fandom. After Supernatural, Kripke created Revolution (NBC, 2012-2014) and Timeless (NBC, 2016-2018) before developing The Boys for Amazon. His partnership with Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg (Point Grey Pictures) brought the Garth Ennis comic to television. Kripke's adaptation significantly reworked the source material, softening some of Ennis's more extreme cynicism while adding contemporary political dimensions that were less explicit in the original comics. His version of The Boys is more accessible and more directly topical than Ennis's work, which was more nihilistic and less interested in being political commentary than in being a middle finger to the superhero genre. The Kripke version wants to say something about contemporary America. Whether you agree with what it says determines how you will receive the show.

Content Breakdown

Adult Viewer Insight

The Boys is a show that rewards adult viewers who can engage with content they disagree with. The craft is undeniable. Antony Starr should have won awards. The show's treatment of corporate power is more sophisticated than most political art and offers genuine insights even to viewers who reject the show's conclusions. The critique of how institutions use patriotism and religion as marketing tools is not wrong just because the show's proposed alternative (deep cynicism about all institutions) is unsatisfying. Conservative adults who can say 'I see what you are doing and I disagree with your conclusion but respect the craft' will find The Boys a richer experience than those who need their entertainment to share their values. The sexual content is extreme and not for everyone regardless of ideology. Preview episode 2 before deciding whether to continue.

Parental Guidance

TV-MA. Not appropriate for children or teenagers under 18. The season contains: extreme graphic violence including body horror; a sexual assault scene in episode 2; full frontal male nudity; an orgy sequence; pervasive profanity (hundreds of F-bombs); sustained critique of religion and patriotism; and thematic content involving corporate manipulation, sexual coercion, drug abuse, and institutional corruption. This is one of the most adult-oriented shows in the streaming landscape. Parents should watch alone before any consideration of shared viewing with older teenagers. Even then, proceed with extreme caution. The show is designed to provoke and disturb. It succeeds.
